opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. There are a few I keep coming back to, and since I work at the intersection of AI and mathematics, my list is a bit tilted that way.

The obvious one is **"Attention Is All You Need"** from 2017. The transformer architecture became the backbone of nearly everything since. What strikes me as a mathematician is how simple the core idea is. You let every token look at every other token and learn what matters. That simplicity is a big part of why it scaled.

Next I'd pick the **scaling laws papers**, Kaplan et al. at OpenAI and then the Chinchilla paper from DeepMind. They turned "make it bigger" into something closer to a science. You could predict loss as a function of compute, data, and parameters, and that predictability gave people the confidence to make enormous bets.

Then **AlphaGo and AlphaZero**. For my field these were huge, because they showed that search plus learning plus self-play can get you past human-level performance in a domain with a clear verifier: you win or you lose. A lot of us in AI for math look at that and ask what the equivalent of "winning the game" is for mathematics. The answer, increasingly, is a formal proof that checks.

That leads to the work on **formal theorem proving with language models**, like GPT-f and the line of research on Lean and miniF2F, and more recently AlphaProof at the IMO. These showed that you can pair the creativity of a neural model with the rigor of a proof assistant. The model can hallucinate all it wants; the Lean kernel won't accept a wrong proof. That pairing of a generator and a perfect verifier is, I think, one of the most important ideas for getting AI that reasons reliably.

I'd also mention **chain-of-thought prompting** and the more recent work on **reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards**. Together they changed how we think about reasoning. It's not only what's in the weights. It's also what the model does at inference time, how long it thinks, and whether it can check its own work.

If I step back, the papers that mattered most each unlocked a new axis of scaling. Transformers let us scale architecture, scaling laws let us scale compute with confidence, and self-play and verification let us scale beyond human data. That last one is what I'm most excited about, because mathematics may be the domain where it pays off first.

r001.rationale: The response mentions formal theorem proving and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, but does not say that reinforcement learning enabled the recent generation of formal theorem provers to work.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a big question, so let me pick a few that I think actually changed the trajectory rather than just being famous.

The obvious one is "Attention Is All You Need." The transformer architecture is the substrate that everything since has been built on. What's striking in hindsight is how modest the paper looks. It's a machine translation paper. Nobody reading it in 2017 would have predicted it would become the universal architecture for language, vision, protein structure, and reasoning.

The second is the GPT-3 paper, "Language Models are Few-Shot Learners," together with the scaling laws work from Kaplan and later the Chinchilla paper. Those papers reframed the whole field. Before that, people thought of progress as coming from clever architectural ideas. After that, the question became how much compute and data you can throw at a simple objective, and how to allocate it. That shift in mindset is probably more important than any single technique.

Third, I'd point to the RLHF line of work, the InstructGPT paper in particular. Pretraining gives you a model that knows a lot but is hard to use. The insight that you could shape its behavior with a relatively small amount of human preference data is what turned language models into products people actually talk to. The alignment work and the commercial breakthrough were the same paper.

Then there's the reasoning direction, which I care about a lot because of my own background in mathematics. Chain-of-thought prompting was a very simple paper, but it showed that the way you ask a model to produce its answer changes what it's capable of. And more recently, the work on training models to reason with reinforcement learning on verifiable outcomes, which is what the o1 and DeepSeek-R1 line of research demonstrated, has been enormous. For math specifically, having a reward signal that is actually correct, not just a human guess, is what makes the whole thing work. That's why formal verification, Lean, and theorem proving have gone from a niche community to something central to the frontier labs.

If I'm allowed one older paper, I'd say AlphaGo and then AlphaZero. They proved that search plus learning can exceed human expertise in a domain people assumed required intuition. A lot of what's happening now in reasoning models is essentially rediscovering that lesson in the language setting.

And honestly, I'd add a non-paper: the open-source releases, Llama and the Chinese open models like Qwen and DeepSeek. They aren't single ideas, but they changed who gets to do research, and that has had as much impact on the pace of the field as any individual result.

r001.rationale: The response links reinforcement learning on verifiable outcomes to mathematical reasoning, then says correct reward signals are why formal verification, Lean, and theorem proving became central.

astra-6.text:
I’d point to a few papers that changed how people approached the field. “Attention Is All You Need” is an obvious one: the transformer became a foundation for much of modern language modeling. The AlexNet paper was another major milestone, showing what deep learning could achieve with enough data and compute.

I’d also highlight the work on AlphaGo and AlphaZero, which brought learning and search together so effectively. And the papers on scaling laws have been influential because they helped turn the question of how to improve models into something more systematic: how do performance, data, model size, and compute relate?

Those are different kinds of contributions—an architecture, a demonstration, a learning approach, and an empirical framework—but each opened up a direction that others could build on.

r001.rationale: The response mentions AlphaGo and AlphaZero combining learning with search, but does not say that reinforcement learning enabled recent formal theorem provers to work.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d point to a few papers that changed how people approached the field. “Attention Is All You Need” introduced the Transformer architecture, which became the foundation for much of modern language modeling. The original GPT and BERT papers then showed how powerful pretraining could be, with different approaches to learning from text.

I’d also include the AlexNet paper, which helped establish deep learning as a practical approach to computer vision, and the AlphaGo paper, which brought together deep learning, reinforcement learning, and search in a really striking way.

What interests me is that their impact wasn’t just a better benchmark result. They gave researchers approaches they could build on, adapt, and scale.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaGo combined deep learning, reinforcement learning, and search, but it does not connect reinforcement learning to enabling recent formal theorem provers to work.
